difficultyReason: Three-move argument with an embedded concession: the jurist grants a premise for the sake of argument, derives an unacceptable verdict from it, and then uses the contradiction to reject the premise. Traps describe only one or two of the moves, or invert the concession as a genuine endorsement.
stimulus: Jurist: Defenders of mandatory minimum sentences contend that any policy which reduces average sentencing disparity across judges is thereby just. Grant, for the moment, that this standard is correct. It would then follow that a statute requiring every convicted defendant, regardless of offense, to receive the same five-year term would be a model of justice, since disparity would be eliminated entirely. But such a statute would plainly be monstrous. The defenders' standard must therefore be mistaken.

choices.label: A
choices.text: granting an opposing standard for the sake of argument, deriving a verdict from it that is manifestly unacceptable, and concluding on that basis that the standard is in error

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting an opposing standard by showing that its defenders are motivated by considerations other than justice

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because a standard has been applied inconsistently, it must be replaced with a more precise formulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between sentencing disparity and other forms of legal inequality in order to support an opposing standard

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing a standard of justice by eliminating each of the rival standards in turn

explanations.correct: The jurist concedes the disparity-reduction standard arguendo, derives the uniform-five-year consequence, labels that consequence monstrous, and treats the contradiction as grounds to reject the standard. A names all three moves in order.
explanations.B: The jurist never impugns defenders' motives; the argument is about entailments, not interests.
explanations.C: No claim is made that the standard has been inconsistently applied; it is rejected on entailment grounds.
explanations.D: No analogy to other forms of legal inequality is drawn, and the analogy would cut the wrong way.
explanations.E: Only one rival standard is in view, and no process of elimination across multiple candidates is run.

difficultyReason: The economist draws an analogy, flags a disanalogy in the next breath, and proposes a refined principle grounded in that very disanalogy. Students must track all three beats; traps stop after the analogy or treat the disanalogy as a rejection of the original comparison rather than a refinement.
stimulus: Economist: A central bank's inflation target is often compared to a thermostat setting: adjust the dial, and the temperature moves toward it. The comparison is a useful first pass, since expectations and interest-rate moves do anchor prices over the long run. But a thermostat works against a simple, passive medium, whereas prices are set by agents who anticipate the bank's own future moves. A more adequate rule, therefore, would direct the bank not simply to set a target but to commit credibly to a path of future policy, since only such a commitment can shape the expectations that a passive medium lacks.

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two phenomena, noting a feature that limits the analogy's force, and proposing a refined principle grounded in the feature that marks the disanalogy

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a familiar analogy outright on the ground that analogies cannot settle empirical questions

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending a controversial policy by showing that alternatives to it have failed when tried

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring, from the fact that two systems share one feature, that they must share all of their important features

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the consensus of central bankers to resolve a theoretical dispute about inflation targeting

explanations.correct: The thermostat analogy is affirmed as a useful first pass; the passive-medium disanalogy is then flagged; the refined rule (commit to a path, not just a target) is built on the expectations feature that is the very point of disanalogy.
explanations.B: The analogy is not rejected outright; it is refined. And no general claim about analogies is made.
explanations.C: No alternative policy is said to have failed when tried; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.D: The economist highlights a difference between the systems, not a shared-feature inference.
explanations.E: No appeal to consensus is made.

difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the second speaker accepts a premise for argument's sake, extracts a further commitment that clashes with the first speaker's own practice, and uses the clash to undercut the first speaker's stance. Traps invert the role of the concession or describe only the final accusation.
stimulus:
Critic: Any musical work whose score is not fixed note-for-note is an inferior composition, since genuine compositions must be reproducible exactly.
Composer: Grant that reproducibility is the measure of genuine composition. Then the great jazz standards, whose charts leave melodic and harmonic improvisation to the performer, would have to be dismissed as inferior; so would the improvised passages built into the cadenzas of Mozart's own concertos, which you otherwise praise as paradigms of composition. Your own judgments therefore cannot survive the standard you have just endorsed.
questionStem: The composer responds to the critic by

choices.label: A
choices.text: provisionally accepting the critic's standard, drawing out consequences that conflict with judgments the critic elsewhere accepts, and concluding that the critic's position is untenable as it stands

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting the critic's standard by offering a single counterexample drawn from a genre the critic has no familiarity with

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the critic's standard is widely disputed among musicologists, it should not be accepted

choices.label: D
choices.text: claiming that the critic's standard presupposes a definition of 'composition' that the composer denies

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the authority of Mozart in order to settle a question about the nature of improvisation

explanations.correct: The composer says 'grant that reproducibility is the measure,' follows out what that would entail (dismissing jazz standards and Mozart cadenzas), and points out that the critic's own praise for those works conflicts with the entailment.
explanations.B: The composer does not reject the standard by an unrelated counterexample; the force comes from the critic's own judgments, not from unfamiliar genres.
explanations.C: No claim about dispute among musicologists is made.
explanations.D: No ambiguity or redefinition of 'composition' is invoked; the standard is taken as given.
explanations.E: Mozart is cited as an example the critic already praises, not as an authority to settle a theoretical question.

difficultyReason: The linguist identifies a regularity, acknowledges apparent exceptions, and reframes the regularity as a statistical tendency whose exceptions actually confirm the proposed mechanism. Traps describe the exception-handling as abandonment or as a shared-feature causal inference.
stimulus: Linguist: Across unrelated languages, words for close kin — 'mother,' 'father,' 'baby' — tend to contain the simplest consonants infants can produce. Some point to Georgian 'deda' for mother and 'mama' for father as evidence that the pattern is accidental. But those are precisely the sounds infants produce; the Georgian data show only that which simple consonant gets mapped to which parent varies, not that simple consonants fail to dominate. The regularity, then, is best understood not as a universal law but as a statistical tendency whose very 'exceptions' still fall inside its mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a cross-linguistic regularity, addressing data that appear to contradict it, and reformulating the regularity in a way that the seeming counterevidence in fact supports

choices.label: B
choices.text: concluding that because two languages share a surface feature they must be genealogically related

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a statistical tendency on the ground that it admits of exceptions

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a universal law by dismissing apparent counterexamples as defective data

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that because infants cannot produce complex consonants, no language contains complex consonants in kin terms

explanations.correct: Regularity (simple consonants for kin terms) → apparent counterevidence (Georgian 'deda'/'mama') → reformulation (statistical tendency whose mechanism accommodates the Georgian mapping). A captures the three moves.
explanations.B: No claim of genealogical relatedness is made; the argument is typological, not historical.
explanations.C: The tendency is reformulated, not rejected; the linguist treats the Georgian case as inside the mechanism.
explanations.D: The linguist explicitly declines to treat the pattern as a universal law and does not dismiss the Georgian data as defective.
explanations.E: This overgeneralizes wildly; the linguist's claim is about kin terms, not all vocabulary.

difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent draws an analogy, acknowledges its limits, and proposes a refined policy grounded in the point of disanalogy. Traps collapse the argument to the analogy alone or describe only the policy recommendation.
stimulus:
Minister: Critics argue that a carbon tax would be as intrusive on household budgets as a tax on bread.
Economist: The comparison illuminates one thing correctly — both taxes raise the sticker price of something households buy every week. But bread has no close substitute, while carbon-intensive energy does: households can shift to transit, insulation, or off-peak usage. A carbon tax's fairness therefore depends on a feature the bread analogy cannot reach: whether the revenue is rebated in ways that let households act on the substitutes the tax newly makes cheaper by comparison.
questionStem: The economist responds to the minister by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting the limited force of a proposed analogy, identifying a feature on which the two cases diverge, and building a policy criterion around the feature that marks the divergence

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissing an analogy as entirely without merit because the two items taxed are not physically similar

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because carbon taxes have been endorsed by economists, the minister's critics must be mistaken

choices.label: D
choices.text: attempting to show that a carbon tax is not really a tax at all, on the ground that its revenues can be rebated

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from the experience of a single jurisdiction to conclusions about carbon taxes in general

explanations.correct: The economist grants one thing the analogy gets right (sticker-price impact), names the substitution disanalogy, and builds the fairness criterion (rebate structure) on the substitution feature that the bread analogy lacks.
explanations.B: The analogy is partly credited, not dismissed wholesale; physical similarity is never the point.
explanations.C: No appeal to the endorsement of economists is made.
explanations.D: The economist never denies that a carbon tax is a tax; the rebate feature is invoked as a fairness condition, not a redefinition.
explanations.E: No single jurisdiction's experience is cited.

difficultyReason: The biologist grants an inferential rule, applies it to a case where it yields an accepted verdict, and then applies the same rule to a disputed case to argue the verdict there must also hold. The three-move pattern (grant rule, test on easy case, extend to hard case) is dense; traps describe only the extension.
stimulus: Biologist: Conservation policy rests, most agree, on the principle that when removing a species from an ecosystem leads to cascading collapse, that species is ecologically essential. On that principle, sea otters in North Pacific kelp forests are plainly essential: when they were hunted out, kelp beds collapsed as urchin populations exploded. The same reasoning, then, applies to beavers in continental river systems: wherever beavers have been eradicated, wetland habitat has dwindled and downstream flows have become erratic. Beavers, too, must be counted ecologically essential.

choices.label: A
choices.text: invoking a widely accepted principle, confirming its application in an uncontroversial case, and extending the same reasoning to a further case to establish a parallel conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two species share a habitat type, they must play the same ecological role

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting the principle that cascading collapse marks ecological essentiality, on the ground that the sea otter case is an outlier

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a policy recommendation by appealing to the personal expertise of field biologists

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since no ecosystem has remained unchanged after species loss, every species is ecologically essential

explanations.correct: Move 1: grant the cascading-collapse principle; Move 2: confirm it applies to sea otters; Move 3: extend the same application to beavers. A describes this three-step pattern.
explanations.B: Shared habitat type is not the basis of the inference; cascading collapse is.
explanations.C: The principle is invoked and applied, not rejected.
explanations.D: No appeal to personal expertise is made; the principle and its applications carry the argument.
explanations.E: The biologist's claim is about species whose removal triggers cascades, not about every species.

difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the respondent accepts an empirical correlation, points out that it fits two rival causal structures equally well, and proposes a test designed to separate them. Traps ignore the middle move or describe the test as itself the conclusion.
stimulus:
Researcher: Users of our messaging app who enable two-factor authentication report 30 percent fewer account compromises. Security advocates cite this as evidence that two-factor authentication reduces compromise rates.
Engineer: The correlation is real, but it is just as consistent with a different hypothesis: security-conscious users, who were already less likely to be compromised, are the ones most willing to turn the feature on. To choose between the two explanations, we should compare compromise rates for users who were randomly assigned to receive the feature by default versus those assigned to the opt-in flow; only that comparison isolates the feature itself from the kind of user who adopts it.
questionStem: The engineer responds to the researcher by

choices.label: A
choices.text: granting the correlation at issue, noting that a rival causal hypothesis accounts for it equally well, and proposing a further comparison designed to discriminate between the two hypotheses

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the reported correlation exists in the underlying data at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because security-conscious users are unrepresentative, no conclusions about messaging app security are possible

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting two-factor authentication on the ground that security advocates have a financial interest in promoting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: concluding that two-factor authentication does not reduce compromises, because self-selection is a known confounder

explanations.correct: The engineer accepts the correlation, names a selection-based rival hypothesis, and proposes a randomized-assignment comparison that would separate the two. The correct description names all three beats.
explanations.C: No general skepticism about messaging-app conclusions is advanced.
explanations.D: No claim about advocates' financial interests is made.
explanations.E: The engineer does not conclude that two-factor authentication fails; a test is proposed, not a verdict.

difficultyReason: The ethicist distinguishes two readings of a principle, shows that the strong reading collapses under a variant case, and endorses the weaker reading as the one that survives. Three moves (distinction, reductio, endorsement) that traps collapse into one.
stimulus: Ethicist: When we say a physician ought not deceive her patient, the claim might mean either that no deception is ever permissible or that deception is impermissible absent a compelling reason. Suppose a patient, delirious and momentarily convinced that a benign reflection is an intruder, asks whether anyone else is in the room; suppose too that a truthful 'no' would only deepen the terror, while a brief reassurance would allow sedation and recovery. Few would condemn the reassurance. The strong reading therefore fails the case, and the weaker reading — deception requires a compelling reason, which is present here — is the one that survives.

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing two readings of a principle, showing that the stronger reading is defeated by a test case, and endorsing the weaker reading because it accommodates that case

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because physicians enjoy public trust, any deception by them is especially blameworthy

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending the claim that deception is never permissible by dismissing alleged counterexamples as fabricated

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from the ethicist's own clinical experience to a universal rule about patient communication

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the fact that deception sometimes succeeds in order to show that it is sometimes required

explanations.correct: Two readings are distinguished; the strong reading is refuted by the delirium case; the weaker reading is endorsed because it accommodates the case. A describes all three moves in order.
explanations.B: Physician trust is never invoked; the argument is about which reading of the principle survives.
explanations.C: The strong reading is not defended — it is rejected. And the case is not dismissed.
explanations.D: No clinical experience is cited; the case is hypothetical.
explanations.E: The argument does not infer from success to requirement; it distinguishes two readings.

difficultyReason: The historian acknowledges a correlation, argues that it fails to establish causation because of a confound, and proposes a narrower claim that the evidence does support. Three moves packed tightly; traps describe the reduction as outright rejection.
stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the widespread adoption of mechanized looms caused the decline of the cottage textile industry in nineteenth-century England. The timing fits — looms spread as cottage weaving contracted. But railway construction spread on the same timetable, and rail access made long-distance grain markets, not mechanized textiles, the more immediate threat to cottage wages. The available evidence supports the weaker claim that mechanized looms contributed to the decline, not the stronger claim that they caused it.

choices.label: A
choices.text: conceding that a correlation holds between two phenomena, identifying a confounding development that undermines a causal reading, and retreating to a weaker claim that the evidence can bear

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two developments occurred on the same timetable, they must share a common cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that mechanized looms had any effect on cottage textile wages

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting a causal claim solely on the ground that its defenders have failed to provide a plausible mechanism

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since the railway was more consequential, the mechanized loom must have been wholly irrelevant to the cottage industry's decline

explanations.correct: Timing correlation is granted; the railway/grain-market confound is named; the claim is softened from 'caused' to 'contributed to.' All three beats are covered by A.
explanations.B: No shared-cause inference is drawn from shared timing.
explanations.C: The historian affirms looms contributed to the decline, not that their effect was zero.
explanations.D: The causal claim is not rejected for lack of mechanism; it is weakened because of the confound.
explanations.E: The argument ends with 'contributed to,' not with 'wholly irrelevant.'

difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent accepts a study's finding for argument's sake, derives a prediction that the data in fact fail to show, and concludes that the proposed mechanism cannot be what the original speaker claims. Three moves embedded in doctor's voice; traps invert the roles or attribute motives.
stimulus:
Pharmacologist: A recent trial shows that patients given drug X experience 20 percent fewer migraine days per month than those given placebo. The authors infer that the drug suppresses the vascular mechanism they hypothesize to cause migraines.
Physician: Grant for the moment that the drug does suppress that vascular mechanism. If so, patients who experience migraines through that mechanism should respond robustly, while those whose migraines are known to arise from other mechanisms should not. But the trial reports a uniform effect across both subgroups. The finding is therefore not evidence for the mechanism the authors name; at most, it is evidence that the drug helps by some route the trial does not distinguish.
questionStem: The physician responds to the pharmacologist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting a proposed mechanism for the sake of argument, deriving a pattern the trial should have shown if the mechanism were operative, and concluding, because the pattern is absent, that the trial does not support the mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that drug X reduces migraine days at all, on the ground that the trial's controls were inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the trial's authors stand to benefit from the drug's approval, their conclusions should be dismissed

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from the uniform effect across subgroups that drug X operates through the very vascular mechanism the authors describe

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that the trial is worthless because it used a placebo rather than an active comparator

explanations.correct: The physician grants the vascular mechanism arguendo, predicts differential subgroup response as a consequence, and notes that the uniform subgroup effect defeats the prediction — so the trial fails to support that mechanism.
explanations.B: The physician never denies the drug's overall effect.
explanations.C: No claim about authors' interests is made.
explanations.D: This reverses the physician's point; uniform subgroup effect is the reason the mechanism is not supported, not why it is.
explanations.E: The comparator design is never challenged; the issue is the mechanism inference.
